title: Amaziah's Pride and Jeroboam's Restored Borders
summary: Amaziah of Judah begins well, punishing his father's murderers without killing their children, and defeats Edom. Swollen by victory, he challenges Jehoash of Israel, ignores a stinging parable, and is captured while Jerusalem's wall is breached and its treasures carried off. Amaziah later dies in a conspiracy, his son Azariah takes the throne, and in the north Jeroboam II, though he keeps the old sins, restores Israel's borders because the LORD saw its bitter affliction.
story: Chapter 13 ended with God's covenant compassion keeping Israel alive and Jehoash winning back cities from Aram. This chapter shows both kingdoms at a turning point. Judah's king overreaches and is humbled by his northern neighbor, a reminder that the division begun under Rehoboam in 1 Kings 12 still festers into open war. Israel, meanwhile, enters its last season of prosperity under Jeroboam II, one of the longest and most successful reigns in its history. The narrator gives that success only a few verses and explains it entirely as mercy. The reader who knows what comes next (six kings in about thirty years, then the fall of Samaria in chapter 17) will feel how thin the ice was under this prosperity.
historical:
Amaziah ruled Judah from about 796 to 767 BC, though his years may overlap with his son's. Jeroboam II ruled Israel from about 793 to 753 BC, probably including a period as co-regent with his father Jehoash. These dates are approximate, and scholars reconstruct the overlapping reigns in different ways. Jeroboam's expansion was possible because Aram-Damascus had been weakened by Assyrian campaigns, while Assyria itself went through a period of internal weakness in the first half of the eighth century and did not press west in force. For a generation, the small kingdoms of the Levant had room to grow.

The prophets Amos and Hosea both date their ministries to the reign of Jeroboam II (Amos 1:1; Hosea 1:1), and their books give the view from below: luxury for the wealthy, oppression of the poor, and worship that went through the motions. Archaeology fits this picture of prosperity. The Samaria ostraca, inked potsherds recording shipments of wine and oil to the capital, are usually dated to the early eighth century, and a fine seal found at Megiddo inscribed as belonging to Shema, servant of Jeroboam, is often, though not universally, assigned to this Jeroboam. The Jonah son of Amittai named in verse 25 is the same prophet whose book tells of his mission to Nineveh.
cultural:
Amaziah's restraint in verse 6 was striking in its world. When a new king took power after an assassination, it was common across the ancient Near East to wipe out the killers' whole families, removing future avengers. Amaziah instead obeys Deuteronomy 24:16, quoted here: “Fathers must not be put to death for their children, and children must not be put to death for their fathers; each is to die for his own sin.” The narrator wants us to see that the law of Moses was meant to shape royal policy, not only temple worship.

Jehoash's reply in verses 9-10 uses a fable, a short animal or plant story with a moral, a form well known in the ancient world (Jotham's fable of the trees in Judges 9 is another). The thistle asking the cedar for a marriage alliance is absurdly presumptuous, and a passing wild animal crushes it without noticing. "Let us meet face to face" could sound like an invitation to talk, but Jehoash hears it for what it is, a challenge to battle. Breaking down four hundred cubits of wall (about 180 meters, or 600 feet) was a deliberate humiliation that left the capital exposed, and taking hostages secured Judah's future good behavior.
literary: The chapter alternates between the two kingdoms using the regnal formulas that structure all of Kings: accession date, age, length of reign, mother's name (for Judah's kings), verdict, annals, and burial. Amaziah's verdict is carefully graded: right in the LORD's eyes, but not like David, and the high places remain. The central episode (verses 8-14) is a small drama in three movements: challenge, fable, and defeat. Its keynote is pride, named in verse 10, where the Hebrew speaks of the heart being lifted up. The Jeroboam section (verses 23-29) has the most compressed verdict in the chapter and then an unusual theological explanation (verses 26-27) that echoes the language of Deuteronomy 32:36, where the LORD sees that his people's power is gone and no one is left, slave or free.

outline.t: Justice for the assassins and victory over Edom
The thistle and the cedar: Judah defeated by Israel
The death of Jehoash of Israel

doctrines.note: Amaziah's refusal to execute the children of his father's killers is explicitly credited to the Book of the Law of Moses. God's law limits the power of kings and protects the innocent, even when revenge would be politically convenient.

Pride is the thread of Amaziah's fall. A real victory given by God becomes the ground of arrogance, and arrogance leads a whole nation into disaster. The chapter shows how quickly success can become the occasion of sin.

Verses 26-27 say that Jeroboam's success came because the LORD saw Israel's bitter affliction and had not said he would blot out its name. God used an unfaithful king to rescue a suffering people, without approving the king's sins.

words.note: Bamah, high place. These were local open-air shrines, often on hills, where sacrifice and incense were offered. Some were dedicated to other gods; many were used in the LORD's name but outside the one place Deuteronomy appointed for sacrifice. Kings repeatedly faults even good kings for leaving them, setting up the reforms of Hezekiah and Josiah later in the book.

Choach, thistle or thorn. A lowly, prickly weed, set against the cedar, the grandest tree of Lebanon. Jehoash's choice of the word tells Amaziah exactly how he ranks Judah's power beside Israel's, and the insult drives the fable.

Machah, to wipe or blot out. The verb is used of wiping a dish clean and of erasing names from a record. Verse 27 says the LORD had not said he would blot out Israel's name. The wording is careful: not yet. The same verb reappears in 21:13, when the LORD says he will wipe Jerusalem as one wipes a dish.

christ: The chapter's link to Christ is thematic rather than predictive. Its mention of Jonah son of Amittai places a prophet on the page whom Jesus himself would later cite: he pointed to the sign of Jonah, three days in the belly of the fish, as a sign of his own death and resurrection (Matthew 12:39-41). The chapter also shows a pattern that runs through the whole Old Testament: God saves a helpless people when there is no one to help, as verse 26 puts it. The New Testament announces the final form of that rescue in Christ, who came to those who could not save themselves. And Amaziah's partial righteousness, right but not like David, keeps the reader waiting for a son of David whose heart would be wholly given to God.

hard.q: Why does God bless Jeroboam II with success when the text says he did evil?
hard.a:
Kings does not hide the tension. Jeroboam keeps the calf shrines at Bethel and Dan, and yet his reign brings Israel its widest borders in generations, in fulfillment of a prophetic word. The narrator's explanation is that the success was not a reward for Jeroboam. It was mercy for a suffering people, and it came because God had not yet decreed Israel's end.

Readers have drawn out two lessons from this. One is that prosperity is not proof of God's approval; Amos, prophesying in these same years, saw the wealth of Samaria as a sign of injustice and announced judgment on it. The other is that God's patience has a purpose. The years of Jeroboam were a space for repentance, and the prophets of the time called the nation to use it. When it did not, the prosperity ended within a generation.

questions: Amaziah obeyed God's law in hard circumstances and then was undone by his own pride after a victory. Why is success often more dangerous to faith than failure?
Jehoash's parable told Amaziah the truth in an insulting way. How do you hear hard truths when they come from people who don't wish you well?
God rescued Israel through a king who did evil. What does it mean for you that God's kindness to you is not proof that everything in your life has his approval?
